title: Mimamsa (ritual as meaning)
hook: a letter drops into a mailbox and the act is over in a second, so how does the answer ever come back?

segments.voice: Yesterday Mimamsa said dharma is known through injunction, the Veda's do this, because no camera can film what an act is for. What did you do simply because it was asked? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

The letter is stamped and sealed. A hand lifts the flap of a blue mailbox, lets go, and the flap clanks shut. That's it. The act of sending took about one second, and it's already over. The hand is back in a coat pocket. And yet somewhere, in a bag, on a truck, in a sorting room nobody will ever see, the letter is still traveling. Weeks later, an answer arrives. So where was the sending, all that time? Mimamsa faced this exact puzzle about ritual. Today we hear its answer, and the name it gave it.
screen: `THE FLAP CLANKS SHUT.` → `THE ACT IS OVER.` → `THE ANSWER COMES LATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the puzzle. The Veda says, in effect, the one who desires heaven should perform this offering. Fine. The offering is done. The fire burns down, the chant ends, everyone goes home. The act is finished, gone. But the result it was for comes much later, maybe after this life. How can something that no longer exists bring anything about? Shabara, in his commentary on Jaimini's sutras, gives the answer. The act, he says, doesn't simply vanish. It produces something unseen, which stays and carries the act forward until its fruit arrives. Its name is apurva. Translators render it as the new thing, the unprecedented: something that wasn't there before the act, and is there after. Go back to the letter. The sending was over in a second, but the letter kept going, out of sight, until the answer came. Apurva is the letter in the bag. Notice what this does to ritual. It means that an act done carefully today isn't wasted when it ends. Something has been set in motion that can't be filmed and can't be argued into being. It's known, Mimamsa says, only because the Veda asks for the act and promises its fruit. That fits yesterday. Dharma was something the senses couldn't see. Apurva is how its good travels through time. Other Hindu schools speak of the lasting effect of action in their own ways, and the word karma covers a great deal of that ground. Mimamsa gave its own careful account, built for the fire and the offering.
screen: `THE ACT IS FINISHED.` · `THE FRUIT COMES LATER.` · `APURVA CARRIES IT.` · `THE LETTER IN THE BAG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust the letter for two minutes. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one good thing you did recently that hasn't come back yet. A kind word, a gift, some care given without thanks. Let it stay unfinished. You don't have to know where it is now, or what it will bring. Just let the act be complete as an act. Each out-breath, let it go a little further. If you pray, you can offer that act, as it is. The bell holds the time.
Mimamsa. In Shabara's account, a ritual act produces apurva, an unseen new thing that carries it forward until its fruit comes.
Your line: Mimamsa, ritual as meaning. Today, do one good thing whose result you won't see, and let it go into the bag without checking the tracking number. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Mimamsa teachers explain, following Shabara's commentary, that a properly performed rite produces an unseen potency, apurva, which persists after the act and brings its promised result in time.

fork.setup: you're a student of Mimamsa. the offering is done, the fire is out, and the result is years away. what connects them?
options: nothing; the act is simply gone
apurva, an unseen new thing the act produced
the priest's memory of the rite
fork.reveal: apurva. in Shabara's account, the act leaves something unseen that carries it forward until the fruit arrives.

original.note: Sanskrit: the new or unprecedented; in Mimamsa, the unseen potency a rite produces.

trapdoor: what you thought: a ritual either works on the spot or doesn't work at all.
what it means: in Mimamsa, the act produces apurva, something unseen that carries it forward to a later result.
what a scholar hears: Shabara's commentary on Jaimini, which develops apurva to bridge the gap between a finished act and a fruit that comes long after.
